posts.title: What Survives a Summary
posts.label: Behavioural
posts.excerpt: Novelty is a supply problem, and the supply went infinite. Summarising is free now, and what a summary removes is exactly the part that had someone in it.
posts.body:
It's 8:29 in the evening in Toronto and I'm in my home office. There are birds going at it in the yard behind my window, louder than they have any business being this late. Something soft and faintly melodramatic is playing in the background, which is apparently the mood I need in order to write anything.

I'm telling you this because it's the one part of this essay that couldn't have been produced any other way. Wherever you are reading this, whatever you were thinking about thirty seconds before you opened it, the odds that it lines up with my Wednesday evening are close to nothing.

That gap is the whole subject.

## Novelty is a supply problem

I crave novelty. New tools, new features, new shiny things, constantly. The brain is built for it, and some of us run hotter on it than others. A few people have found something like contentment with what they have and a few have detached from wanting entirely, but most of us sit at the end of the curve where new is the thing we chase.

Here's what I keep circling. Novelty is a supply problem, and the supply went infinite.

Video, audio, podcasts, blogs, threads, whatever arrives next. It pours. You cannot be bored anymore, not in the digital world, and the more of it that lands the more the brain trains itself to want the next one. On top of that, summarising is now free. One query and you have the shape of almost anything.

But a summary smooths. That is its actual job. It takes the specific voice, the lived quarter, the real room with real people in it, and hands back the average. ==What a summary removes is precisely the part that had someone in it.==

## Nobody spends a hundred thousand dollars on a summary

More summary means more options, and more options means more decisions. That's the part that gets skipped when people talk about all of this getting easier.

Watch what large organisations still do. They pay serious money to third-party analysts for reports they could mostly assemble themselves now, faster, at their desk. They aren't buying the information. They're buying the confidence to sign.

I have still never seen an agent make a large purchase decision. Not because the reasoning is beyond it. Because of where the weight sits.

> When somebody decides to spend a million dollars, or to open their heart, or to walk away, only a human feels where that lands.

You can give an agent a spend limit. Some companies are building exactly that and it will work fine. But the decision to raise the limit stays human, because raising it means weighing a set of consequences nobody wrote down anywhere.

A few years ago I stitched together some HTML, CSS and JavaScript to get a landing page up, mostly to prove to my co-founders at Neat that I was technical enough to be in the room. Now I tell Claude what I want and it builds the thing, and I spend the recovered hours on the talking instead. The conviction. Whether the person across from me actually believes it. ==The work didn't shrink. It moved to the part that was always harder.==

## The category arrives before the person

Specificity shows up in how we look at each other too, and this is where I catch myself most often.

Someone tells you something. You hear the high notes, the big beats, and then your brain does the thing it is best at. It sorts. It files them into a category, and from that point on you're reading the category instead of the person. I think this is roughly what Kahneman was describing, and I'll hold that loosely, because I'm working from memory.

So somebody brings you a specific problem and gets a pre-configured response. Oh, they're complaining again. "Yeah, totally, I hear you." ==You answered the box, not the person standing in front of you.==

The alternative is slower and it isn't complicated. Look at them. Work out whether they want to be heard, or validated, or genuinely understood, because those are three different requests and we keep treating them as one.

## You are not built to be everywhere

I spent part of this afternoon on a bench by the lake with a pair of binoculars.

There were small boats out on Lake Ontario. With the naked eye you get all of them at once, drifting, arranging themselves, and there's a flow across the whole field that you can feel without looking at any one thing in particular.

Then I raised the binoculars and the field disappeared. What I got instead was one boat. About twenty feet, a tall mast, and I got caught on the way the ropes ran down to the starboard and port sides. Red drapes. A single red line along the middle of the hull. One inscription on the whole boat, in big bold letters: R12.

I kept coming back to it. I couldn't tell you what was special about R12, only that having gone all the way into that one boat left me with something the wide view hadn't given me in twenty minutes of looking. ==You can have the field or you can have the boat. That isn't a flaw in the binoculars.==

The obvious objection is capacity. You can't be that specific with everyone.

Correct. You can't. That's the point.

You are not a system that absorbs an unbounded number of tokens and finds the pattern. You are a biological instrument that feels heat in one chest about one specific thing and then follows it. ==That limit isn't a defect to engineer around. It's the instrument.==

In any organisation there are a handful of people and a handful of things that genuinely matter this week. Being specific with those is available to you. Being specific with all of it is not, and reaching for it anyway is how you end up specific with nothing.

The question I keep turning over is how this survives contact with a hundred thousand customers. I can't sit with all of them. Nobody can.

What I've found is that going deep with a well-chosen few gets you most of the way there, because the pains converge. Stacks have converged. Nearly everyone is running a similar shape of thing under a different brand. What hasn't converged is what each person pictures as the fix. ==The problems rhyme. The imagined solutions never do.==

## What it looks like on the page

This is also, I think, why some writing works and most doesn't.

When a piece is specific, you get walked through it. The plot develops while you're inside it and you come out the other end with whatever you made of it, without ever feeling you sat through something intellectual. When it isn't specific you're being addressed from above by a sanitised account of how things supposedly went, and there's nothing in it to hold onto.

The strange part is that specificity is what makes writing universal. It works through the body, and the body is the part we all have. The tightness in the chest when something is off. The small flip in the stomach when something warm might be about to happen. The particular satisfaction of finishing something you set your mind to. ==You reach what's common to everyone by going all the way through what happened to exactly one person.==

I read autobiographies for this. Not for the lessons. In hindsight every life looks coherent and the lessons are mostly assembled afterwards. I read them because they're specific. The moment a life becomes an average, an aggregate, a statistic, there's nobody left inside it.

## Carlo, eight months old today

One more thing about specific moments. They're getting harder to come by, and I don't think that's an accident.

I moved to this city recently. Making friends in a big city is possible and it is not easy, and everybody knows this. You have to put yourself out there, you have to take the specific action. But a lot of how society used to work ran on unplanned proximity. You met people because you happened to be standing there. Those random moments had a way of tying up loose ends that the scheduled ones never reach.

The organised specific moment is fine. The random one is what becomes a story. It's the one people are still telling years later, the kind that leaves you feeling you were in the room for it.

So I try to make them on purpose now, using whatever is around me.

Later the same afternoon I met a mother and her baby at a park. I stayed and watched him take his bottle, play, laugh and cry, and at some point I asked her how old he was and what he was called, and whether she was enjoying the park. His name is Carlo. He's eight months old, and today was his eight-month birthday. We talked about the squirrels for a bit. She wished me well. That's the whole event.

It left me warm for hours.

I couldn't have read that anywhere. It doesn't aggregate into anything. No statistic contains Carlo, and nothing was ever going to hand him to me, because the only way to get that was to be standing there paying attention.

Work is the same. It's the hint of sadness in a colleague's eye while they tell you everything is fine, and whether you're specific enough to slow down and take one breath instead of moving to the next thing.

==These are the things that survive a summary.==

posts.title: Liked or Trusted
posts.label: Product Thinking
posts.excerpt: A PM owns the outcome and none of the people, so the instinct is to absorb everything and call it collaboration. That makes you a container. The alternative is a mirror, and it costs you something.
posts.body:
There was a stretch where I'd wake up around three in the morning with my mind already running. Requests, pings, a thread I hadn't closed, four people waiting on me for something. Not a nightmare. Just the queue, going by itself.

I don't think that's unusual. Read a PM forum for ten minutes and burnout is most of the conversation. What gets me is that we don't treat it as a design problem. We amplify it. Everyone passes the anxiety along and the constant pinging gets treated as a sign that people care.

I think the cause is structural, and I think most of us make it worse by accident.

## What a product manager actually owns

Picture three circles. Engineering, business, sales, with design drifting into engineering at most companies now. Around them sits a wider ring: legal, finance, vendors, customers. The PM sits in the middle and moves things between them. Information mostly, but also context, intent, pressure, ideas.

There are two stories about that seat.

One says the PM is the CEO of the product. It sounds great on paper and it was in most of the books I read before I got into this.

The other says the PM does the grunt work. Owns the outcome, does whatever it takes, cleans up after everybody.

Both stories skip the same fact. ==You own the outcome and you own none of the people.== You can't hire anyone, fire anyone, promote anyone or tell anyone what to do. What you own is influence.

## Why the absorbing starts

An engineer's output is legible. The code exists or it doesn't. Sales is legible, the revenue landed or it didn't. A leader has targets with their name on them. A PM has the outcome of a product, which is real but arrives late, and by then a dozen people have touched it.

So you reach for the one thing you can show immediately. Coverage. Being in every room, unblocking every thing, answering inside a minute.

There's a status layer under it too. I've been watching black and white films from the forties, where the people who appear to run the company are the ones in suits doing the selling, and whoever writes the technical work sits somewhere in the back, unseen. That has completely inverted. Mostly for the better, and it still leaves the PM as the person in the middle with the least legible job in the building.

## I was a container

I did this to myself.

Picture the container as an actual bin, and you're dragging it behind you like a trawler. You go to sales and they pour in. You go to engineering and they pour in. Leadership pours in. To survive that you'd need enormous capacity, and nobody has it, so it ends one of two ways. You burn out, or you keep faking it and complain privately in a forum somewhere.

I came into an organisation running distributed infrastructure at scale, with real revenue targets and an undercurrent of anxiety running through everything. Systems broke, because that's what systems do. A large customer would land, the excitement would be genuine, and within a week it had turned into anxiety about the thing we'd just won.

I absorbed all of it. I thought I was being collaborative. I thought I was being liked. Marketing would send me a deck and I'd add two lines to it. I jumped in everywhere, on everything.

What it cost me was that I never said the obvious sentence. ==You're asking us to do this, so what are we giving up for it?==

Without that sentence you run in every direction until you're thin. Then you vent. I'd bundle it up and take it to my manager, and that felt like a release valve. It isn't one. Your manager is one person, and moving the weight upward isn't the same as putting it down.

## How the brake actually gets applied

I wrote an essay a while back about who applies the brakes on reliability, and I argued the brake is always a person, someone willing to say slow down. What I didn't write was what applying it looks like on an ordinary Tuesday.

It looks like a mirror.

Someone brings you a request with weight on it. Instead of taking the weight, you hand it back. What are we giving up for this. How long has this been building. Why is this coming up right now, this week, from you.

> A no puts the weight back where it belongs. It drops an anchor in a room that was drifting.

Not this quarter, and here's what's already in the timeline. Not today, I'm out, I'll come back to you Thursday. And the reason underneath can be that my energy is spent, or I'm on leave, or I'm looking after someone at home, or I'm with people I love. That is core work. It doesn't need a business justification stapled to it.

## Liked or trusted

That's the whole question, and I think every PM has to answer it out loud at some point. ==Do you want to be liked or do you want to be trusted?==

The do-whatever-it-takes camp is usually made of people pleasers who brought the habit in with them. The strange part is it doesn't even buy peace. It generates more chaos. Engineering gets a stream of course corrections and pushes back, correctly. You lose the ability to find signal because every request arrives at the same volume. You get reactive and shallow, you stop having a vision, and you end up performing competence while you're drowning.

The real job is smaller and harder than the drowning version. Sell the vision. Hold a strategy. Align execution through a cadence people can rely on. Talk properly to the customers who actually matter, because you can't talk to all of them and you can't be in every meeting, and pretending otherwise is how the whole thing collapses.

## The mirror points in every direction

Mirror engineering's concerns when you're talking to the business. Mirror the business back to engineering. Show reliability debt to the people holding the revenue number, in language that lands.

It works with customers too, and this is the part people skip. Don't just soak it up and nod. Reflect the weight of the pain back and see whether it actually moves. Sometimes a customer asks for an API change they don't need, because the field they want can already be computed on their end with a small adjustment to what they're already calling. You only find that by holding the mirror steady instead of writing the ticket.

If you're in the camp that says the PM is the CEO of the product, then start there. ==The CEO of the product is the CEO of himself first.== Emotionally, psychologically, and in the specific sense of being able to say no.

## Presence, and what it isn't

There's a reason this matters more now than it did five years ago. A lot of what used to make a PM valuable is getting cheap. The synthesis, the research, the first draft of everything. Intelligence is rentable. ==What isn't rentable is the centre of gravity that lets you hold your own heat steady in your chest while you reflect something difficult back at someone who outranks you.==

I called it coverage earlier. Being everywhere, replying fast, touching everything. That's what I mistook for presence for years, and it's closer to the opposite of it.

==Presence isn't going deep in every conversation, and it isn't getting to all of them. It's being entirely in the one you're actually in.== You can't do that while dragging the bin. That's the whole reason the container fails. It's technically in the room and it isn't there at all.

I noticed something a few days ago. I can stay with a quiet intensity now, with someone, when the moment needs it. I'm not the easygoing one who takes on whatever arrives anymore. Some people feel the sting of that and pull back. That's the cost of becoming real, and I've decided it's worth paying.

This is what I think a PM should actually bring. Not artifacts. Not more noise, more yeses, more things done fast. You're not a task rabbit. You lead with heat, intention and a vision, you reflect a no back when one is needed, and you show people the real state of things so timelines and trade-offs and decisions can be made without flinching.

And real presence builds something. ==It creates a shared reality, and shared reality compounds into meaning.== That's the part missing from most work. That's what I missed. Without it you get a quick hit, and when the hit fades the organisation goes and finds the next people to produce the next one.

It's also what makes anything last. Businesses, communities, relationships, the traditions that outlive whoever started them. None of that gets built by a container.

I'm not a saint about this. I still catch myself wanting to please, wanting to say yes to all of it, wanting to soak it up and be the easy one to work with.

The difference is that I see it now, and I choose differently.

posts.title: How Was Your Weekend
posts.label: Inner Work
posts.excerpt: A friend calls it ethical gossip and claims it's the glue of societies. She's right. The ethics live in two places: what happens to a story once you pass it on, and whether you can hold someone else's without reaching for your own.
posts.body:
It's just after two in the afternoon and I'm on the phone with a friend when she says the words *ethical gossip*. She says them with real joy, laughing, like she's been waiting for a chance to use them.

Her claim is that ethical gossip is the glue of societies. Not a metaphor she's reaching for. The actual glue. It's a big claim and I should have argued with it, but a deep part of me knew immediately what she meant.

I've known her a long time. We don't talk often, but when we do it's like no time passed. I've watched her become an astute lawyer over the years, and her energy is the infectious kind. She's the person who brings social warmth into a room and wants everyone in it connected to everyone else. So of course this idea is hers.

I asked her what she meant by it. She gave me example after example of what happens when someone opens up to a friend under serious circumstances, and how much old emotion comes loose when they do. The examples were personal, so they stay out of this.

What stuck with me was the term. I asked why she liked it so much and she said it's more sensational. Spicier. ==It invites more heat.== She's right, and I spent the rest of the call trying to think of a better word and failing.

## What vulnerability does to the space between people

Here's where my brain went while she was talking.

Gravity is mass bending the space around it. Put two large bodies near each other, the earth and the moon, and the shape of spacetime between them changes. They aren't reaching for each other. The field they're sitting in is curved.

Vulnerability does that to a conversation. Someone says the true thing, at the right moment, to a person they trust, and the space between them bends. You feel it happen. ==Nobody is trying harder. The field just changed shape.==

I felt it on that call, in my chest. Relief, which is a strange thing to feel about someone else's story.

## We are much less unique than we'd like

Earlier in the same conversation we'd been talking about archetypes, and she told me something from her life that was eerily close to something from mine. Not the details. The details were completely different. The shape was the same. The same arc, the same sequence, in an area of life where you'd expect randomness to make every version different.

That's the second thing gossip does. It shows you the pattern.

The feeling of being unique doesn't survive many of those conversations. We vary in how we express things, and the exact time and place is never the same, but we are running a small number of shapes. ==Most of what feels singular about your life is a common form you happen to be living from the inside.==

That sounds deflating written down. In the moment it's the opposite. It's the most relief available.

## Where it breaks

So I asked her the obvious question. In what environments does this break down?

She said that's exactly where the ethical part lives, and gave me two boundaries.

The first is the chain. You go from first-hand observer to second-hand teller to third, and ==in replication lies inherent loss.== You copy and you don't paste exactly. You embellish with your own material. Your biases ride along, your state of mind that day, whatever you needed the story to mean. By the third telling the intent is muddy, and the person at the centre of it has no idea what's being said about them.

The second boundary is harder, because it's about when you *should* share. Sometimes it genuinely matters that a thing gets said, and then it takes conviction and courage to say it, on behalf of the person you're in the conversation with. Silence isn't automatically the ethical choice.

That's the part that left heat in my chest. It's a real ethic, with a cost on both sides of it.

## The side nobody publishes

In corporate settings we do a sanitised version of this and call it sync and align.

People already talk freely about the good parts. We publish those. The launch, the promotion, the trip. Ethical gossip is the other channel, the one for the material people don't want to say out loud, the part with shame on it. ==Shame is where the energy is, which is why that conversation moves something and the other kind doesn't.==

Most of our talking is the same repetitive goddamn thing. How was your weekend. Great, how was yours. There's a place for that. It just isn't load-bearing.

## Are you the moon or the sun?

My friend kept asking me this on the call. She meant it about the energy between two people, how one of you runs hot while the other reflects, and how that arrangement shifts over time.

I took it somewhere else.

When someone hands you the raw thing, you get to choose which one you are for the next ten minutes. You can be the sun and produce your own light, which usually means finding your matching story and telling it. Or you can be the moon and reflect theirs back until they can finally see it.

> Both feel like connection from the inside. Only one of them is.

==When you rush to match someone's story with your own, you fuse, and the other person loses the chance to be seen as distinct.== That's the failure mode, and it's the well-meaning one, which is what makes it hard to catch.

So what I'm left with are questions about capacity.

How much can you carry without passing it on? How much without bleeding your own story in and using theirs as the setup for yours? Can you hold someone else's material while staying present and keeping your own balance? Or does the sight of raw meat light up the neural circuitry that wants to go find a matching story of your own?

All societies are built on gossip. The only live question is how ethical the gossiping has been.

I never did find a better word. I'm leaving this one where it is, in tribute to my friend, because gossip still carries this stink and that's the taste I wanted you to have while reading it.

posts.title: Who Applies the Brakes
posts.label: Systems
posts.excerpt: Is reliability a cultural problem or a technical one? The practices are known and the people are good, and it still breaks. What's left is whether anyone in the room is allowed to say slow down.
posts.body:
Is reliability a cultural problem or a technical one?

I've been sitting with that question since my last quarter running security infrastructure at scale, and I've come to think the answer decides how much reliability a company actually gets. Not how much it says it wants. How much it gets.

Every serious organization is a software organization now. Payments, identity, security, healthcare, telecoms, government, the non-profits quietly running on someone else's stack. If your company matters to anyone, something you don't fully control is holding it up. Security people talk about the [cyber poverty line](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P8RP4QcygzY), and it's a blunter idea than it sounds: a huge number of organizations simply don't have what it takes to defend themselves. No security leadership, or no strategy, or no ability to act on the strategy they have. They know the recommended action. They cannot take it. Sitting under that whole conversation is reliability.

## Nature is reliable. Software is not.

I came into software from chemical engineering, and that background left me with a strange instinct about this. In a plant you have process control: you watch every input and output and hold the system stable while it runs. Underneath all of it sits physics, which is the most reliable thing there is. Gravity does not have an off quarter. The laws hold, and you can verify them.

Software is not that. Software has people in it.

And distributed systems are hard for reasons that have nothing to do with anyone being careless. You're holding state across machines, replicating data inside a region and across regions, watching the latency that costs you and trying to claw it back. Absorbing attacks while you do it. Making sure failovers actually fail over. Carrying the physical risk of real infrastructure, plus every vendor upstream and downstream you don't control. Each one is a place the system can surprise you.

==Reliability isn't a feature you finish. It's a running process, and running processes drift.==

## You can't start here

Here's the tension, and I've lived both sides of it. When you're building zero to one, reliability is not the job. The job is proving an assumption: does anyone want this, what's the smallest thing that produces a real outcome, how fast can someone feel value. I sat in that seat at Neat, and if you'd told me to put a fifth of my capacity into disaster recovery I would have laughed and kept shipping. Correctly.

So no, you can't build reliability in from day one. What you can do from day one is smaller and cheaper: disaster recovery, high availability, safe releases, decent release engineering practice. That shrinks the surface area where incidents happen. It doesn't remove them. Nothing removes them.

Then the company grows, and the surface area grows faster than the discipline does.

## The loudest voice in the room

This is where I stopped treating it as an engineering question.

Companies get built by people running hot. Founders start with a ferocity that's genuinely infectious, and that energy is why the thing exists at all. Now add AI agents writing and shipping code at a speed we haven't had before. If you're growing, reliability is the last thing on your mind. You know you should be thinking about it. You aren't.

And direction gets set by whoever holds the most powerful voice in the room. The CEO, the sales leader, whoever anchors the group. That voice is rarely the one asking about replication lag.

The uncomfortable part is that being smart doesn't save you. I've worked alongside dozens of exceptionally good engineers and watched systems break anyway. Every company operating at real scale has this story. The ones you've heard about are just the ones big enough to make the news. ==Nobody can predict the future, and most reliability failures are that fact arriving on a Tuesday.==

So if the practices are known and the people are good and it still breaks, what's left is the culture. What the organization actually rewards.

## Somebody has to apply the brakes

Here's the image I keep coming back to.

Building fast is momentum, and momentum is physics. It doesn't care about your intentions. The faster you're moving, the more violent every course correction becomes. And you get a lot of course corrections: a big new customer, a new director with a mandate, a competitor's launch, some tool everyone decides is the future this month. Someone is always saying go, go, go, like there's a pack of hungry dogs behind you and a piece of meat somewhere out ahead.

What that produces is zigzagging. Motion that looks like speed and functions like survival. Sometimes it's defensive, sometimes it's the opposite, a lunge at whatever the loudest person saw this week. It depends who's steering, and everyone else spends the quarter reacting to them. I keep a note on my board about not confusing motion with progress, and this is the version of it I've actually lived. ==The chaos doesn't stay in the meetings. It ships.==

> Reliability is the brake. And the brake is always a person, someone willing to say slow down.

You don't apply the brake to stop. You apply it so you can turn without losing the car.

When we finally gave reliability a dedicated slice of a quarter, the surprising part wasn't the refactoring, or the architectural calls that took load off the system. It was the calm. Having one named, protected place where the question got asked changed how the rest of the roadmap felt. It became something we could point at with customers too.

## The twenty percent

Here's the number I'd defend, caveat first.

If you're a startup, ignore all of this. Put a hundred percent into growing the product. Anything else is garbage advice and I've been there.

But if you run at scale, with distributed infrastructure and customers whose businesses sit on top of you, hold twenty percent of the roadmap for reliability. The other eighty is everything else: strategic bets, the CEO-sponsored feature, the sales-sponsored one, the customer signal a PM dug up and defended and decided to bet on. All of it belongs.

The twenty is ongoing work on the architecture as you scale, plus room to react. ==You can move the number. Fifteen is the floor. At ten you're not thinking about reliability, you're just responding to whatever already broke.==

And it isn't always refactoring. Some quarters the work is forensic: what performance actually did over the last three quarters, what volume is coming, how your vendors are scaling, because their ceiling becomes your ceiling. Some quarters there's nothing to do at all and you spend it on features. That means it's working.

## The brake has a word

So: cultural or technical?

Both. But the culture leads, because the technical problem doesn't arrive on its own. People build the system. The pressure they were under, the corners the loudest voice told them to cut, the quarter where nobody was allowed to say slow down, all of it gets built in. The way we build is what eventually shows up as the outage.

And if culture is the lever, then the brake has a word, and the word is no.

Applying the brake looks like one person with enough standing to say no to a specific thing in a specific week. No, that feature doesn't go out this quarter. No, we're not taking that timeline. No, we don't ship on top of this until the replication story holds.

But a no that stops there is obstruction, and obstruction loses every time to someone holding a revenue number. ==The no only works when it arrives with what happens instead.== This is the load we're taking off the hot path. This is the failure we won't survive at next year's volume, and this is the quarter we deal with it. That's the difference between a PM who blocks and a PM who steers.

Reliability is painful. It's boring to fund and invisible when it works, right up until it's the only thing anyone is talking about. Which is exactly why it needs a person and not a policy. The systems will keep drifting, because that is what running systems do, and nobody is coming to predict the future on our behalf.

So somebody in the room has to be willing to be the brake, and to say clearly what the slowing is for. If that person isn't you, find out who it is. If there isn't one, that is your reliability strategy, and you already know how it ends.

posts.title: What My Cat Taught Me About Control
posts.label: Inner Work
posts.excerpt: As a PM you carry the outcome and almost none of the levers, and the urge to control everything gets loud. My cat taught me which parts to actually hold, and which to let go.
posts.body:
It's been foggy in the city for days. Not real fog. Smoke, drifting down from the wildfires up in northern Ontario, thick enough that the air quality reading has been sitting a notch below the number where they tell you to stay inside. I'm on the rooftop anyway, watching the sun go down through the haze, and there's nothing I can do about any of it. A fitting place to think about control.

I'm a control freak. It's obvious to me, and if you're the kind of introspective person who reads essays like this, it's probably obvious to you too. There's a part of us that wants to hold everything in place. It runs hottest in people who grew up somewhere unpredictable, and unpredictable can mean a lot of things: money, affection, safety, whether the ground under you stays where it was yesterday. I won't dig into where mine comes from. That's not the point. The point is that it lives in all of us, and it shows up loudest exactly where it helps least.

## The brain hates not knowing

Here's the thing I keep coming back to. Your brain's main job is prediction. It runs on patterns and will grab any pattern it can find, and when there isn't one, it doesn't shrug and wait. It invents one. That drive runs so deep that uncertainty itself can land as something close to physical pain. Not a figure of speech. A real signal, in the body.

Once you see that, a lot of behaviour stops looking irrational. ==Known misery feels safer than unknown possibility, and a bad plan beats no plan.== On a team it looks like this: instead of someone saying "I don't know," which is honest and leaves room to actually find the answer, people manufacture one. Precisely wrong answers, defended hard, because a confident wrong answer scratches the itch that "I don't know" leaves open. That's the control drive at its finest.

It's also why we build things nobody needs. Why else do useless artifacts get made, circulated through meeting after meeting, nodded at, then quietly abandoned the moment the next fire starts? They were never really about the work. They were about having something to hold.

## What Oona wouldn't do

When I decided to get a cat, I pictured company. I did not picture another consciousness with its own instincts, running on logic completely separate from mine, even though we'd end up sharing the same air.

This was my first winter in Toronto. Early startup days, a roommate, a big glass box of an apartment, and me mostly alone in it. My nervous system wanted that little animal close. So I'd call Oona over. And she would look at me and decline.

It made me furious, in a way I'm slightly embarrassed by now. I fed her. I cleaned up after her. I did everything for her. And she still wouldn't come when I wanted her to. So I did what the control reflex tells you to do. I started thinking about leverage. I'm bigger. I hold the food. I could withhold things and get a reaction, basically run her like a Pavlov experiment.

==Training is not the same as controlling.== You can shape behaviour and still be nowhere near the thing you actually want, which in my case was for her to choose me.

## The manager with no leverage

I think about that apartment a lot now, because product management is the same trap with a bigger cast.

A PM carries the outcome and owns almost none of the levers. You can't fire anyone. You can't discipline anyone. You can't hand the pressure you're feeling to another function and make it theirs. You're standing in the middle of engineering, design, leadership, sales, each guarding its own domain, and you are, if we're honest, an influencer with a big title doing your best to look like you own results you have no direct authority over. They call you the CEO of the product, a strange and double-edged thing to call someone who can't make anyone do anything.

So everyone reaches for the one thing they can hold: their own turf. Design protects design. Engineering protects engineering. Collaboration turns into a round-robin of people restating the same points louder, defending position, because control is what gives us the feeling of order. And underneath it, nobody wants to say the quiet thing: the whole system is fundamentally unpredictable. A reliability incident, someone's life event, an ego collision, and business-as-usual is gone for a week.

## What's actually yours

Here's where I've landed, and I think it's the whole thesis. ==Giving up control, on purpose, is the move.== Not everywhere. Strategically.

There's a small set of things a product person genuinely controls, and the vision is the big one. Not because you can force it into being, but because it's built from work that's entirely yours: the introspection, the information you gather, the customer conversations, the sleeping on it and chewing on it, and then the leap. Listening to the heat and pouring it out before you can prove it's right. That zero-to-one act is yours.

You can control the inputs too, and this is where the last two years change the picture. A lot of what used to eat a PM's week is now fast: synthesizing user feedback, pulling market research together, drafting the value proposition and the user journeys, standing up a rough prototype and shipping it to see what happens. The work bends toward judgment and trust and away from grinding raw material by hand.

Everything past that, the people, the timelines, the outcome itself, you hold with an open hand. The way I eventually held Oona. I stopped trying to make her come, let time and trust do their slow thing, and we found a cadence. She couldn't control me and, honestly, I don't think she was ever trying to. I was the one gripping. The moment I stopped, the relationship came back.

## The performance trap

There's a version of the control reflex I'm still catching in myself, in this essay even.

When I started writing, years ago, I would over-research and over-rewrite and obsess over every line. I told myself that was rigor. Looking back it was control over how I'd be seen. I wanted the smart, authoritative image instead of just being a person who went through something and set it down plainly. I was performing.

> Performance is control wearing a nicer jacket. You can't perform without managing the image, the tone, the whole impression.

Then there are the apps. I've used all of them, from plain long lists to software that promised to make me superhuman, and every time the tool became one more thing to manage and optimize. There was a stretch of a few quarters where I tracked almost everything: what I did, a backlog, every idea, days and weeks and months planned tightly enough that life would surely become predictable. Fuck, the irony of that lands differently now that I'm writing it down. I'm not against the tools. I still use them. I've just stopped letting them talk me out of the truth that chaos is a built-in feature of the whole thing, and that everyone I see, including me, is wearing a mask. Performing. (If you prefer your pain written in corporate jargon.)

## The other side is autonomy

Under the need to control is its twin, and everyone has it. Oona had it. Every colleague has it, regardless of title. We crave order, and we crave autonomy just as badly, the room to use our own judgment without someone's hand on us.

The strongest teams I've seen make peace with this. They don't treat conflict as a threat to be smoothed over. They let it exist, hold a lot of trust, and get very clear about the narrow set of things they can control and the large set they can't. That freedom is what lets them build under real uncertainty.

The question I keep circling, and I don't think this essay answers it, is what happens as more of us work alongside AI. If autonomy of judgment becomes the scarce, valuable thing, does the machine we hand tasks to want autonomy too? I don't know. But whenever I feel the grip tightening, in a standup, in a comment thread, in myself, I try to remember it's usually just the heat. The thing in your chest that flares when you think your idea or your voice or your weight is about to be taken. Everyone feels it. Everyone gets defensive. And pointing it out in someone else is the oldest move there is, because naming it makes you sound like the one person in the room who isn't doing it.

Let that sit with you. That's the heat.

posts.title: Ship Fast, Sit Still
posts.label: Inner Work
posts.excerpt: Everyone thinks shipping fast means running hot. The teams that actually move build in a quieter half: the introspection that tells you whether the motion means anything.
posts.body:
When people hear "startup" and "ship fast," a certain picture shows up. A room that runs hot. People talking over each other, the loudest idea winning, everyone a little over-caffeinated and performing urgency. Somewhere we decided a bias toward shipping has to look like that. Reactive, loud, always moving.

I've been in enough of those rooms to know the energy is usually a performance.

## When fast is actually slow

Here's what actually happens in the reactive version. Ideas get repeated instead of examined. Someone says a thing they heard somewhere, someone else says it back, and it circulates until it sounds like conviction. Garbage in, garbage out. The room feels productive because it's busy, and busy gets mistaken for thoughtful.

These teams tell themselves they move fast. Often they're the slowest ones in the building. They break things quickly, yes, and they also build a pile nobody uses, then burn the next quarter cleaning up after a thing they shipped before they understood it. A boat at full throttle with nobody on the rudder still moves fast. It just doesn't get anywhere on purpose.

There's a quieter irony too. These rooms usually aren't psychologically safe. When every silence gets filled with noise, the person who needs a beat to think doesn't get the beat. So you lose the one input that would have saved you the wasted quarter.

## Where my bias to ship comes from

I should be clear that I love shipping. My bias toward action is real, and it isn't for show. It comes from Aba, the city in southeastern Nigeria where I grew up, hustling with my family to help cover school fees. Acting on imperfect information wasn't a philosophy there. It was how you ate. You move, you learn, you adjust. I trust that instinct more than almost anything I have.

So this isn't an argument against moving fast. It's about the thing that has to sit next to it.

## The other half lives in the same container

The inward part. The self-development work every one of us has to do if we're going to keep growing as people. Introspection gets a bad name because from the outside it looks like nothing is happening. Someone sitting still, not producing, not talking. In a go-go-go room that reads as idle, sometimes as a liability.

But introspection looks like the opposite of shipping only until you understand what it does. It's the sensor that makes shipping worth anything.

Picture it as the internal balance of the system. Your emotional state. What you're actually trying to build, and why. The thought process you're running, with its biases and blind spots riding along. The wider context you're sitting inside. When you can see your own internal reality clearly, you hold on to the outer one too.

> Introspection is the internal rudder. Without it, the ship still moves fast, just in whatever direction the last gust pushed it.

That rudder is what lets you sail continuously instead of lurching from gust to gust. It's also what lets you take the real bet, the courageous one, before all the data is in.

## You can't trust the heat if you won't sit with it

I've written before about the heat. The signal in your chest that flags when something matters, when a bet is worth the risk, when you're about to make a mistake. Innovation runs on that signal, because innovation asks you to act before you can prove you're right.

Here's the part people skip. You can't trust your gut if you've never learned to sit with it. You can't read the heat if you can't stay still long enough to feel where it points. ==The instinct everyone wants to "just trust" is built in the quiet, not in the noise.== The reactive room trains you out of the very skill it claims to run on.

## What leaders show, and what they hide

The strangest version of this lives at the top.

Leadership in a lot of companies performs a single mode. The energetic CEO, the supercharged director, the whole push-push-push register. That's the part that gets seen, so that's the part that gets copied down the org. Everyone learns that intensity is the job.

What almost never gets shown is the other side. The long hours of alignment. The quiet work of holding a vision steady while the details churn. The reflection that goes into a decision before it's announced with confidence. The leaders I've watched actually succeed have serious introspective practices. You don't see them, because that work happens with the door closed. And because it stays invisible, it doesn't get modeled, and so it doesn't get practiced.

That's what I want to name. ==We've made the performance of shipping into the whole culture, and left the inner half of the work out of view.==

## Both, held at once

You don't have to choose between the two. The bias to ship gets you moving. The introspection keeps the movement honest, and keeps you able to feel, even in the noise, which bet is actually worth making. I'm still learning to hold both at once. Most days the work is just staying quiet long enough to feel where I'm actually pointed.

posts.title: What a Chemical Engineer Knows About Product
posts.label: Systems
posts.excerpt: How did a chemical engineer end up in product? Mass balance, process control, and thermodynamics turn out to be a strong education in shipping software — and in the one thing agentic AI can't rent: the heat.
posts.body:
"How did you get into product?" I get this a lot — from friends, family, coworkers. Chemical engineering and software look like different planets, and when I was actually making the jump, I couldn't have told you how they connected. I didn't have a story. But hindsight assembles one whether you ask it to or not — which is its own lesson, and maybe the first principle here: the throughline is usually only visible looking back.

So here's the one I see now.

## Everything is a balance

Stripped down, chemical engineering is the study of moving and transforming things — mass, energy, heat — and keeping them balanced while you do it. Mass balance, energy balance, thermodynamics, fluid dynamics, process control. The "product" could be anything: a reaction, a stream of heat, steam turned into power, raw material turned into finished chemical.

Software products are dynamic systems too. Sometimes they're deterministic — the system has a job and you control for that outcome. Sometimes they have to guess what a human wants, and those equations are far messier than anything in a thermodynamics textbook. But the instinct is identical: account for the variables that matter, and don't over-engineer the ones that don't.

## Start in the petri dish

You don't model an entire plant to run a reaction in a test tube. You start small — molecules in a small tube — and only scale to the thousand-cubic-metre-a-day plant once you understand the process. And the most important balance early on isn't heat or pressure. It's effort: *how little can I build to learn something real?*

The first version of any piece of software has one job, and it isn't to solve the whole problem. ==Its job is to gather data and clarify assumptions.== You go from unknown to known. We didn't start a reaction with process modeling on day one — you earn the right to model once the reaction works. Product is the same.

## Reliability is a process, not a feature

At Cloudflare the systems were already at scale — closer to a running plant than a test tube. So I shipped two ways. Some features went straight into the process engine, the massive distributed system. Others were gated: experimental, released to a single customer, validated, cleaned up, *then* rolled out.

A chemical plant runs continuously through stages — combustion, transfer, transformation, storage, filtering, distillation — and process models watch every input and output to keep it stable. A large distributed system is the same organism. Chemical engineering teaches you this before you ever touch software: **the reliability of the process is sacred.** When something runs at scale and people depend on it, that lesson stops being optional.

## Listen to the heat

Here's the part I didn't expect to carry with me.

Thermodynamics doesn't stop at pipes and reactors. Heat moves through every system — including the human one. I've come to treat the people who build and use software, myself included, as thermodynamic systems. And I've learned to listen to the heat.

> Heat is information.

You know the feeling. Something makes you angry and your chest tightens. An idea excites you — or terrifies you — and you feel it in your body before you can explain it. Heat itself is nothing; it's a transfer of energy, the thing that moves other things. But it points. It flags when you're upset, when you're about to make a mistake, when an idea matters enough to scare you.

Innovation runs on that signal. Taking a real product bet means acting before the data is 100% — a courageous translation of an idea into something real that isn't validated yet. That's not recklessness; it's what experimentation is. The leap needs a gut, and the gut speaks in heat. Chemical engineering gave me the math and physics of heat. What it left me with is an appreciation for the version I feel in my chest right before I make a quick bet.

Not every bet lands. That was never the point. ==Innovation isn't being right; it's having the courage to turn an idea into something real before anyone can prove it will work.==

## When intelligence is rentable

I didn't set out to write about AI here. But the question underneath this whole essay — what actually transfers? — has never mattered more.

Today, knowledge and intelligence can be rented. Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini — you can skip almost all of "the stuff": the derivations, the modeling, the first ten drafts. What you can't rent is the thing that starts the process — initiative, intention, the spark someone has to strike. And you can't rent the heat.

You can't press a button, go to sleep, and wake up to a finished thing that mattered. That's the world we're told to expect. But the heat — the signal that says *this* bet, *this* idea is wrong, *this* one is worth the risk — only shows up inside a physical body. Agentic AI can run the process. It can't feel the chest tighten. ==Intelligence is rentable now; the heat is not.==

So the chemical engineer's lesson doesn't retire in the age of AI — it sharpens. When the process gets cheap, the whole game becomes knowing which process to start, and being the body in the room that can feel whether it's working.

I couldn't have drawn this map on the way in. But maybe that's the point: the process only teaches you what it's doing while it's running. You just have to stay close enough to feel the heat.

posts.title: Held With Confidence, Never Rigidity
posts.label: Product Thinking
posts.excerpt: A roadmap isn't a contract — it's a sequenced hypothesis. Now, next, later; held with confidence, reviewed every quarter, never locked.
posts.body:
## Principle

In an ever-changing world, roadmaps represent an attempt at certainty, and any PM who holds too tightly to them runs the real risk of failing to react quickly, failing to innovate, and damaging relationships across the organization — with sales, support, customer success, executive leadership, and engineering alike. At best, the roadmap is a best guess. It needs to be named that, communicated that way, and treated that way. ==The artifact you commit to is not a contract; it is a sequenced hypothesis — what's *now*, what's *next*, and what's *later* — reviewed every quarter, held with confidence but never with rigidity.==

## Elaboration

This principle does not mean planning is worthless or that conviction is optional. An appropriately flexible PM has still done the thinking. They've mapped customer pain points, stated assumptions, estimated impact, and brought reasoning to the table. The act of presenting a roadmap already signals conviction. The difference is they also build in explicit space — a percentage of capacity, a dedicated bucket — for uncertainty, for inbound signals from sales or a major enterprise on-ramping, for reliability work that wasn't visible until a billion queries started failing at 2 a.m.

The principle breaks down in predictable, legitimate places: regulatory deadlines like FedRAMP High certification that span multiple quarters and require every team in the company, major platform migrations, and customer-committed contracts. In those situations, "it's just a best guess" is the wrong framing — **those are deadlines you work backward from, not guesses you iterate toward.** But even then, the remaining capacity still belongs to experimentation, and any org operating at that scale should protect at least one team or one slice of every PM's time that is *not* locked to a committed deliverable. That's where the next big thing comes from.

To a skeptical CFO or board member worried about accountability and investor confidence: the worry is legitimate. But unless there is a regulatory deadline, a committed contract, or a platform migration consuming capacity, a roadmap built on unvalidated assumptions and fast customer feedback loops — some of them moonshots — is exactly the mechanism that produces the next inflection point. ==Best-guess roadmaps backed by real customer pain and stated assumptions are not chaos; they are disciplined experimentation.==

The tell for a PM using flexibility as cover for poor planning is simple: they can't show their reasoning. An appropriately flexible PM can walk you through *why* something is on the roadmap, what assumption it's testing, and what signal would cause them to move it. A PM hiding behind uncertainty can't do that. **They're not flexible — they're just unplanned.**

For the artifact itself: *now / next / later*, each item annotated with a confidence level, the assumption being tested, and the potential impact if the assumption holds. That gives every stakeholder — engineering, sales, leadership — enough to plan around without creating the illusion that anything beyond the current quarter is locked.

## Example

A while back, the team had just closed one of its largest enterprise customers, with a huge and fast-growing volume of traffic running through the system. Revenue was growing. Leadership was excited. Board meetings were full of good numbers, and the roadmap was stacked with new features chasing that momentum.

What got lost was reliability. The architecture had extra round-trips baked into a check sitting in the hot path. Fine at low volume, a bottleneck at scale. A piece of code written quickly to satisfy a customer request introduced a bug that started locking users out. Incidents stacked, and the biggest customers started losing trust.

Looking back, the last real load test on record was years old. The performance commitments made to customers had been set on numbers nobody had re-validated under the new load.

Afterward, a significant portion of the roadmap for the following quarters went to reliability. Not because leadership mandated it, but because the pain was visible to the customers that mattered most, and leadership felt it too. Reliability work was mapped against active engineering efforts already in flight, so it read as an overlay rather than a detour. The lesson wasn't to abandon growth-oriented roadmapping. It was to always hold a dedicated bucket for infrastructure, reliability, and the things that don't show up as feature requests until something breaks. ==The roadmap had been treated as a growth plan. It needed to also be a system health plan.== Both are best guesses. Neither can be ignored.

posts.title: Building AI agents at Cloudflare: what actually worked
posts.label: AI / MCP
posts.excerpt: The agents that get adopted aren't the most capable — they're the ones that replace one painful task so reliably people stop thinking about them.
posts.body:
I built a production MCP agent during my time at Cloudflare, and scoped a second. Here's what I learned about what makes an agent actually useful versus impressive.

The first agent — the one we shipped — indexed internal wikis, the codebase, API docs, and architecture diagrams to answer cross-platform technical questions. It replaced hours of context-gathering with a reliable shortcut that engineering and PM teams started using daily.

The second agent I scoped and architected: it would pull customer data from our CRM, usage metrics from Grafana, and market signals to give sales teams a live brief on account health before conversations. I got deep into the data model and tooling design before I left, but it wasn't shipped during my tenure.

What I noticed from the first agent: the agents that get adopted aren't the ones with the most impressive capabilities. They're the ones that replace a specific, painful, repetitive task with a reliable shortcut. People didn't care about the architecture. They cared that they could stop spending 20 minutes before every call compiling context.

The lesson: the best AI agent isn't the one that can do the most — it's the one that does one thing so reliably that people stop thinking about it and just use it. Tool design and reliability beat capability breadth every time.

The second lesson: the hardest part of agent development isn't the model or the tooling. It's the data quality and retrieval. Our knowledge agent was only as good as how well our internal docs were maintained. Garbage in, garbage out — no matter how good the LLM.

posts.title: What Rory Sutherland taught me about product decisions
posts.label: Behavioural
posts.excerpt: Logic is a terrible guide to human behaviour — and to funnels.
posts.body:
I've read Alchemy four times. Each time I find something new that changes how I think about why features succeed or fail — and it's rarely the thing you'd optimise for.

Sutherland's central argument is that logic is a terrible guide to human behaviour. People don't make decisions on utility — they make them on perception, context, and irrational signals that logic would dismiss. The book is full of examples where the 'logical' solution was wrong and an 'illogical' one worked brilliantly.

The lesson I keep coming back to in product work: before you optimise a funnel, ask whether the funnel is actually what's driving the behaviour you want. Often it isn't. The friction isn't in the UI — it's in the signal the UI is sending.

When I was at Neat, we had a retention problem. The 'logical' fix was to improve onboarding. We tried that. It didn't move the number. What moved it was adding a single social proof element at exactly the right moment — not because it added information, but because it changed the psychological context of the decision. That's Sutherland in practice.

The same principle applied at Cloudflare. Some of our best feature adoption came not from making things easier, but from making them feel more intentional and powerful. Enterprise buyers aren't just buying function — they're buying confidence. The signal you send about your product matters as much as the product itself.

posts.title: DNS security for PMs: what you actually need to know
posts.label: Security
posts.excerpt: Start with the buyer's anxiety, not the technology.
posts.body:
Most PM resources on DNS security are either too shallow or too technical. This is the version I wish I'd had when I joined Cloudflare.

DNS is the phone book of the internet. When you type a domain, your device asks a DNS resolver: 'what IP address does this map to?' That lookup happens before any connection is made — which means it's one of the best places to enforce security policy.

DNS filtering works by intercepting those queries and applying rules: block this category, allow that domain, flag this pattern. At Cloudflare, we did this at L3/L4 (network layer) and L7 (application layer), giving enterprise customers granular control over what traffic enters and leaves their networks.

The PM insight that took me a while to learn: DNS security isn't just about blocking bad sites. For enterprise customers, it's about visibility and policy enforcement across a distributed workforce. The 'block' is almost secondary to the audit log, the analytics, and the ability to prove compliance. That's what CISOs actually buy.

If you're moving into security PM from another domain: start with the buyer's anxiety, not the technology. The technology is learnable in weeks. Understanding why a CISO loses sleep — and how your product changes that equation — takes longer and matters more.

posts.title: Valentine's Day, the sun, and a cat called Oona
posts.label: Life
posts.excerpt: Coffee, sun, 678 quadrillion photons, and a gentle lady.
posts.body:
Instagram is full of couples today. Carefully curated, or faux-silly — everyone performing love for the feed. I used to do this too.

Instead I'm on my Queen Street rooftop. Coffee. Sativa. Sun. The fog this combination creates is useful — it softens the sharp edges of things. Feelings. Thoughts. The unpleasantness we all carry but rarely sit with.

My friend V ran us through a sun ritual this morning. Simple: stand in it. Let it soak you. Then she started talking about photons — 678 quadrillion of them per square inch per second, racing 93 million miles in 8.5 minutes. Massless. Chargeless. Both wave and particle. They drive photosynthesis, colour, that feeling of warmth on your skin. Pure energy, delivered for free, without prejudice. All you have to do is show up and receive.

I keep thinking about that. Show up. Receive.

She mapped the chakras onto wavelengths of light: root chakra red at 630nm, through to crown violet at the top. Whether you believe the chakra part or not, sitting in the sun and thinking about light this way hit differently.

Then I came home to Oona.

We adopted her in April 2022 when I was alone over the holidays, deep winter, middle of lockdown. She was born November 2021 and named "Candy" by the shelter — a funny and terrible name for a cat. I renamed her Oona.

We didn't always get along. My ego wanted to establish hierarchy. She made it abundantly clear she answers to no such thing. She's truer to her instincts than any power game I tried to run. Eventually I yielded. We became friends.

These days she cuddles up next to me when I sleep. Visits when I call. Patiently waits when I serve breakfast at 11am. A gentle lady who still knows how to set a boundary.

I never thought I'd be a cat dad. But on this Valentine's Day, the love I'm celebrating is hers.

Happy Valentine's Day, Popoon.
